::: {.incremental}
- Non-technical stakeholders curious about AI's impact on analytics
- R developers looking to adopt AI-assisted workflows
- Teams managing analytics projects at scale
:::

::: {.notes}
Frame this early — the presentation works on two levels. Non-technical folks will get the "what's possible" picture; developers will leave with enough to get started themselves.

## The High-Level Workflow

```{=html}
<div class="workflow-steps">
```

1. Write a **PRD** (Product Requirements Document) with Claude
2. Break the PRD into **GitHub Issues**
3. Implement iteratively using **Claude Code**
4. Review, sign off, and close issues

```{=html}
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
This is the spine of everything. Each section of the talk maps onto one of these steps. Keep it high level here — we'll unpack each part as we go.
:::

## Prompt Engineering — Why It Matters

::: {.incremental}
- How you ask is as important as what you ask
- Vague prompts produce vague, unpredictable results
- Structured prompts give you consistent, repeatable outputs
- Particularly important in long-running analytics projects where requirements evolve
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the mindset shift. Think of prompting less like typing a search query and more like briefing a capable colleague — context, constraints, and expected output all matter.
:::

---

## Prompt Engineering — Techniques & Resources

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Skills-based prompting**

Matt Pocock's approach: reusable, named prompt patterns for recurring tasks

- `/grill-me` — Claude interrogates your idea before you build
- `/write-a-prd` — structured requirements before a line of code
- `/prd-to-issues` — PRD broken into actionable GitHub issues
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why this works**

- Reduces ambiguity at the start
- Catches gaps before they become bugs
- Creates an audit trail of decisions
- Non-technical stakeholders can review and contribute
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Matt Pocock has been developing a set of Claude Code skills that operationalise good prompting habits. Worth pointing the developers in the audience to his work directly.
:::

## Case Study — Planning the To-Do App

*We'll build this live — here's the process we'll follow*

::: {.incremental}
- Start with `/grill-me` — Claude interrogates the requirements
- Use `/write-a-prd` — capture what we're building and why
- Run `/prd-to-issues` — PRD becomes a set of GitHub Issues
- Each issue is a self-contained unit of work with a clear definition of done
:::

::: {.notes}
The live demo picks up from here. This slide sets up what the audience is about to watch — frame it as showing the plan before executing it.
:::

---

## Case Study — Building & Iterating

*Live coding — Claude Code takes the issues one at a time*

::: {.incremental}
- Hand each GitHub issue to Claude Code individually
- Claude reads the issue, writes the code, runs checks
- Review the output before closing the issue
- Course-correct mid-build when needed — that's expected, not a failure
:::

::: {.notes}
Emphasise that this is a collaboration, not automation. Claude does the heavy lifting but the developer is steering throughout.
:::

---

## Ralph Loops — Autonomous Iteration

> "An infinite loop that repeatedly feeds the same prompt to an AI coding agent — until the work is done."
> — Geoffrey Huntley, [ghuntley.com/loop](https://ghuntley.com/loop/)

::: {.incremental}
- Each iteration starts with **fresh context** — no memory of previous runs
- Progress lives in **your files and git history**, not the LLM
- Only works well with feedback loops: type checks, tests, CI
- After each run, learnings are written back to `AGENTS.md`
:::

::: {.notes}
Named after Ralph Wiggum — stumbles forward with naive confidence. That's a feature, not a bug. The key insight is that state lives in your repo, not the model.
:::

---

## Managing Context & Memory

::: {.incremental}
- Every Claude conversation has a **context window** — a limit on what it can hold in mind at once
- Long sessions drift: early decisions get forgotten
- Strategies:
  - Keep sessions focused on one issue at a time
  - Use `CLAUDE.md` for persistent project-level memory
  - Reset the conversation when switching tasks
  - Summarise and carry forward only what's needed
:::

::: {.notes}
This is where many people hit their first wall. Explain context window simply — "imagine Claude can only read the last N pages of a book at any time." CLAUDE.md is the fix for project conventions and preferences.
:::

---

## GitHub Issues as Memory Store

::: {.incremental}
- GitHub Issues act as **persistent state** across sessions
- Structure issues so Claude can pick up where it left off
  - Clear title and acceptance criteria
  - Links back to the PRD
  - Comments capturing decisions made mid-build
- When you start a new session, point Claude at the open issue
- Nothing is lost between conversations
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the practical answer to the context window problem. The issue IS the brief. Every new Claude session gets the same starting point.
:::

---

## GitHub Issues as Quality Sign-Off

::: {.incremental}
- Issues double as a **review and approval workflow**
- Non-technical stakeholders can read, comment, and approve
- Closing an issue = definition of done
- Builds an audit trail: what was built, when, and why
- Particularly useful in regulated or team environments
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that lands with non-technical stakeholders. They get to participate meaningfully without touching code. Frame it as making quality everyone's job.
:::

---

## Limitations — When Claude Isn't the Right Tool

::: {.incremental}
- **Real-time or streaming data** — Claude doesn't connect to live sources
- **Highly specialised domain knowledge** — deep actuarial, clinical, or legal domain nuance still needs a human expert
- **Complex statistical methodology** — Claude can implement a method, but choosing the right one is yours
- **Ambiguous or shifting requirements** — garbage in, garbage out; structure the problem first
- **Sensitive or confidential data** — know your organisation's data policy before sharing context with any AI
:::

::: {.notes}
Being honest here builds trust with both audiences. Developers will appreciate the nuance; stakeholders will feel reassured that humans are still in the loop where it counts.
:::

---

## Cost Considerations

::: {.incremental}
- Claude charges by **tokens** — roughly, words in and words out
- Context window usage is the biggest cost driver
- Ways to manage cost:
  - Keep sessions focused (shorter context = fewer tokens)
  - Use Claude Code's subscription for regular development work
  - Reserve API calls for automated or high-volume tasks
- Frame it as **time saved vs. cost**: even at full price, an hour of Claude is cheaper than an hour of developer time
:::

::: {.notes}
Don't be coy about the fact that this costs money. But do frame the ROI clearly — the question isn't "does this cost anything?" it's "does it cost less than the alternative?"
:::

## Getting Started

**What you need**

- R and RStudio (or VS Code)
- A Claude Code subscription
- A GitHub account

**Recommended first steps**

1. Install Claude Code
2. Try `/grill-me` on your next project idea
3. Write a PRD before writing any code
4. Open your first GitHub Issue and hand it to Claude Code

::: {.fragment}
*The best way to learn this is to build something real.*
:::

::: {.notes}
End on action. Give the developers in the room something concrete to do this week. Non-technical folks leave knowing what to ask their teams about.
:::
